claim: AWS Client VPN is a managed client-based VPN service that lets you securely access your AWS resources and resources in your on-premises network from any location using an OpenVPN-based VPN client.
q: What is AWS Client VPN in one sentence?
v: a managed client-based VPN service that enables you to securely access your AWS resources and resources in your on-premises network
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/what-is

AWS Client VPN is a managed client-based VPN service that enables you to securely access your AWS resources and resources in your on-premises network. With Client VPN, you can access your resources from any location using an OpenVPN-based VPN client.

claim: The Client VPN endpoint is a Regional construct that you configure. The VPN sessions of the end users terminate at the endpoint.
q: Is a Client VPN endpoint Regional or global, and what ends there?
v: The Client VPN endpoint is a regional construct
The VPN sessions of the end users terminate at the Client VPN endpoint
ev: www/vpn/faqs
The Client VPN endpoint is a regional construct that you configure to use the service. The VPN sessions of the end users terminate at the Client VPN endpoint.

claim: A target network is a subnet in a VPC. A Client VPN endpoint must have at least one target network so that clients can connect to it and establish a VPN connection.
q: What is a Client VPN target network and how many does an endpoint need?
v: A target network is a subnet in a VPC
must have at least one target network
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/cvpn-working-target
A target network is a subnet in a VPC. An AWS Client VPN endpoint must have at least one target network to enable clients to connect to it and establish a VPN connection.

claim: For IPv4 traffic, Client VPN applies source NAT: the source IP address from the client CIDR range is translated to the IP address of the Client VPN network interface. For IPv6 traffic, SNAT is not applied.
q: What source IP address do resources in the VPC see for traffic from Client VPN clients?
v: the source IP address from the client CIDR range is translated to the Client VPN network interface IP address
For IPv6 traffic, SNAT is not applied
scope: Client VPN traffic sent to the VPC
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/what-is

For IPv4 traffic, source network address translation (SNAT) is applied, where the source IP address from the client CIDR range is translated to the Client VPN network interface IP address. For IPv6 traffic, SNAT is not applied, providing enhanced visibility into the connected user's IP address.

claim: When you associate a subnet with a Client VPN endpoint, a route for the VPC is automatically added to the endpoint route table. To reach other networks you must add a route manually.
q: Which routes does a Client VPN endpoint have after you associate a subnet?
v: a route for the VPC is automatically added to the Client VPN endpoint's route table
you must manually add a route to the Client VPN endpoint's route table
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/cvpn-working-routes

When you associate a subnet from a VPC with a Client VPN endpoint, a route for the VPC is automatically added to the Client VPN endpoint's route table. To enable access for additional networks, such as peered VPCs, on-premises networks, the local network (to enable clients to communicate with each other), or the internet, you must manually add a route to the Client VPN endpoint's route table.

claim: To enable connectivity to other networks, add a route to the specific network in the Client VPN route table and add an authorization rule that enables access to that network.
q: What do you configure so Client VPN users can reach a peered VPC or an on-premises network?
v: add a route to the specific network in the Client VPN route table
add authorization rule enabling access to the specific network
ev: www/vpn/faqs
To enable connectivity, add a route to the specific network in the Client VPN route table, and add authorization rule enabling access to the specific network.

claim: For internet access through Client VPN, add an authorization rule for 0.0.0.0/0, and make sure the route table of the associated subnets has a default route that targets an internet gateway or a NAT gateway.
q: What is needed so Client VPN clients can reach the internet through the VPN?
v: For access to the internet, add an authorization rule for 0.0.0.0/0
the route table for the associated subnets has a default route that targets either an internet gateway or a NAT gateway
scope: Client VPN endpoint with full tunnel
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/no-internet-access
For access to the internet, add an authorization rule for 0.0.0.0/0.
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/no-internet-access
If you do not get a response, make sure that the route table for the associated subnets has a default route that targets either an internet gateway or a NAT gateway.

claim: AWS Client VPN supports ports 443 and 1194 for both TCP and UDP. The default is port 443.
q: Which ports does Client VPN support and which is the default?
v: ports 443 and 1194 for both TCP and UDP
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/what-is
AWS Client VPN supports ports 443 and 1194 for both TCP and UDP. The default is port 443.

claim: By default the Client VPN endpoint uses the UDP transport protocol; you can choose TCP at creation. You cannot change the transport protocol after you create the endpoint.
q: Which transport protocol does a Client VPN endpoint use by default and can it be changed later?
v: By default, the Client VPN endpoint uses the UDP transport protocol
You cannot change the transport protocol after you create the Client VPN endpoint
cond: choose TCP when you create the endpoint
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/cvpn-working-endpoint-create
(Optional) By default, the Client VPN endpoint uses the UDP transport protocol. To use the TCP transport protocol instead, for Transport Protocol, select TCP.
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/cvpn-working-endpoint-create
You cannot change the transport protocol after you create the Client VPN endpoint.

claim: AWS Client VPN supports authentication with Active Directory using AWS Directory Service, certificate-based authentication, and federated authentication using SAML 2.0.

v: authentication with Active Directory using AWS Directory Services
ev: www/vpn/faqs
AWS Client VPN supports authentication with Active Directory using AWS Directory Services, Certificate-based authentication, and Federated Authentication using SAML-2.0.

claim: You can use one Client VPN authentication method alone, or combine mutual authentication with a user-based method. If you combine them, both methods must be used to authenticate.

both methods must then be used to correctly authenticate in VPN
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/client-authentication
You can use one of the preceding methods alone, or you can use a combination of mutual authentication with a user-based method such as the following:

q: Do you need a server certificate in ACM for every Client VPN endpoint?
v: you must provision a server certificate in AWS Certificate Manager
regardless of the type of authentication that you use
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/client-authentication
To create a Client VPN endpoint, you must provision a server certificate in AWS Certificate Manager, regardless of the type of authentication that you use.

claim: Client VPN integrates with Directory Service to authenticate clients against existing Active Directory groups, in AWS or on premises. For an on-premises Active Directory without an existing AWS Managed Microsoft AD, you must configure an AD Connector.
q: How does Client VPN authenticate users against an on-premises Active Directory?
v: Client VPN provides Active Directory support by integrating with Directory Service
you must configure an Active Directory Connector (AD Connector)
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/ad

Client VPN provides Active Directory support by integrating with Directory Service. With Active Directory authentication, clients are authenticated against existing Active Directory groups. Using Directory Service, Client VPN can connect to existing Active Directories provisioned in AWS or in your on-premises network. This allows you to use your existing client authentication infrastructure. If you are using an on-premises Active Directory and you do not have an existing AWS Managed Microsoft AD, you must configure an Active Directory Connector (AD Connector).

claim: Client VPN supports multi-factor authentication (MFA) when it is enabled for AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector, and when it is enabled in your SAML identity provider.
q: Does Client VPN support MFA?
v: Client VPN supports multi-factor authentication (MFA) when it's enabled for AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is supported when it's enabled in your IdP
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/ad
Client VPN supports multi-factor authentication (MFA) when it's enabled for AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector.
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/federated-authentication
Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is supported when it's enabled in your IdP.

claim: With mutual authentication, Client VPN uses certificates to authenticate between the client and the server. You must upload the server certificate to AWS Certificate Manager and specify it when you create the endpoint.
q: How does Client VPN mutual authentication work?
v: Client VPN uses certificates to perform authentication between the client and the server
You must upload the server certificate to AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and specify it when you create a Client VPN endpoint
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/mutual
With mutual authentication, Client VPN uses certificates to perform authentication between the client and the server.
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/mutual
You must upload the server certificate to AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) and specify it when you create a Client VPN endpoint.

claim: Client VPN supports a statically configured Certificate Revocation List (CRL), so you can block specific client certificates.
q: Can you revoke a client certificate for Client VPN?
v: AWS Client VPN supports statically-configured Certificate Revocation List (CRL)

ev: www/vpn/faqs
Yes, AWS Client VPN supports statically-configured Certificate Revocation List (CRL).
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/security-best-practices
Use client certificate revocation lists to revoke access to a Client VPN endpoint for specific client certificates.

claim: Client VPN supports identity federation with SAML 2.0, so users connect with centralized credentials from an identity provider. A Client VPN endpoint supports a single IdP only.
q: How does Client VPN support single sign-on, and how many identity providers can an endpoint use?
v: AWS Client VPN supports identity federation with Security Assertion Markup Language 2.0 (SAML 2.0)
A Client VPN endpoint supports a single IdP only
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/federated-authentication

AWS Client VPN supports identity federation with Security Assertion Markup Language 2.0 (SAML 2.0) for Client VPN endpoints. You can use identity providers (IdPs) that support SAML 2.0 to create centralized user identities.
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/federated-authentication
A Client VPN endpoint supports a single IdP only.

claim: With SAML-based federated authentication, users must use the AWS provided client to connect, and a third-party OpenVPN client cannot be used.
q: Can a third-party OpenVPN client connect to a Client VPN endpoint that uses SAML federated authentication?
v: Users must use the AWS provided client to connect to the Client VPN endpoint
you must use the AWS Client VPN software client to connect to the endpoint
scope: Client VPN endpoints with federated authentication
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/federated-authentication
Users must use the AWS provided client to connect to the Client VPN endpoint.

No, you must use the AWS Client VPN software client to connect to the endpoint.

claim: Client VPN supports two types of client authorization: security groups and network-based authorization using authorization rules.
q: Which two kinds of authorization does Client VPN use?
v: two types of client authorization: security groups and network-based authorization (using authorization rules)
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/client-authorization
Client VPN supports two types of client authorization: security groups and network-based authorization (using authorization rules).

claim: For each network you want to enable access to, you configure an authorization rule with the Active Directory group or SAML-based IdP group that is allowed. Only users in that group can access the network.
q: How do you limit which Client VPN users can reach a network range?
v: you configure the Active Directory group or the SAML-based IdP group that is allowed access
Only users who belong to the specified group can access the specified network
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/client-authorization

For each network that you want to enable access, you must configure authorization rules that limit the users who have access. For a specified network, you configure the Active Directory group or the SAML-based IdP group that is allowed access. Only users who belong to the specified group can access the specified network.

claim: By default there are no authorization rules, and access to a destination network is denied until you add an authorization rule. You cannot add an authorization rule to restrict access to a network.
q: What is the default access in Client VPN without authorization rules?
v: The default behavior is to deny access
You cannot add an authorization rule to restrict access to a destination network
cond: add authorization rules to allow access
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/cvpn-working-rules
To allow access to a destination network, an authorization rule must be explicitly added. The default behavior is to deny access.
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/cvpn-working-rules
You cannot add an authorization rule to restrict access to a destination network.

claim: When you associate a subnet with a Client VPN endpoint, AWS automatically applies the default security group of the VPC. To limit an application to Client VPN users, allow access only from the security group applied to the association.
q: Which security group is applied to a Client VPN subnet association and how do you restrict an application to Client VPN users?
v: we automatically apply the VPC's default security group
allow access only from the security groups that were applied to the associated subnet
cond: you can change the security groups later
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/client-authorization
When you associate a subnet with a Client VPN endpoint, we automatically apply the VPC's default security group.
www/vpn/faqs

claim: A client connect handler lets you run custom logic that authorizes a new connection based on device, user and connection attributes. Currently the only supported type of client connect handler is an AWS Lambda function.
q: How can you add custom connection authorization logic to Client VPN?
v: run custom logic that authorizes a new connection, based on device, user, and connection attributes
the only type of client connect handler that is supported is a Lambda function
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/connection-authorization

You can configure a client connect handler for your Client VPN endpoint. The handler enables you to run custom logic that authorizes a new connection, based on device, user, and connection attributes.
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/connection-authorization
Currently, the only type of client connect handler that is supported is a Lambda function.

claim: By default all traffic from Client VPN clients is routed over the VPN tunnel. With split-tunnel turned on, only traffic destined for a network that matches a route in the endpoint route table goes over the tunnel.
q: By default, does all client traffic go through the Client VPN tunnel, and what changes with split tunnel?
v: all traffic from clients is routed over the Client VPN tunnel
only traffic with a destination to the network matching a route from the Client VPN endpoint route table is routed over the Client VPN tunnel
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/split-tunnel-vpn

By default, when you have a Client VPN endpoint, all traffic from clients is routed over the Client VPN tunnel. When you enable split-tunnel on the Client VPN endpoint, we push the routes on the Client VPN endpoint route table to the device that is connected to the Client VPN endpoint. This ensures that only traffic with a destination to the network matching a route from the Client VPN endpoint route table is routed over the Client VPN tunnel.

claim: Split-tunnel lets only AWS-destined traffic use the VPN tunnel, and it reduces the volume of outgoing traffic from AWS, which reduces the data transfer cost.
q: How does split tunnel reduce Client VPN cost?
v: You can reduce the volume of outgoing traffic from AWS, therefore reducing the data transfer cost
having only the AWS destined traffic traverse the VPN tunnel
ev: docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/split-tunnel-vpn
You can optimize the routing of traffic from clients by having only the AWS destined traffic traverse the VPN tunnel.
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/split-tunnel-vpn
You can reduce the volume of outgoing traffic from AWS, therefore reducing the data transfer cost.

claim: By default, split-tunnel on a Client VPN endpoint is disabled. You can turn it on for a new or an existing endpoint.

You can enable split-tunnel on a new or existing Client VPN endpoint
cond: enable at creation or modify later

To have the endpoint be a split-tunnel Client VPN endpoint, turn on Enable split-tunnel. By default, split-tunnel on a Client VPN endpoint is disabled.
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/split-tunnel-vpn
You can enable split-tunnel on a new or existing Client VPN endpoint.

any routes manually added to the Client VPN endpoint's route table

claim: The client CIDR range cannot be changed after you create the Client VPN endpoint, and you should plan twice the addresses you need for the maximum concurrent connections.

a CIDR block that contains twice the number of IP addresses that are required

A portion of the addresses in the client CIDR range are used to support the availability model of the Client VPN endpoint, and cannot be assigned to clients. Therefore, we recommend that you assign a CIDR block that contains twice the number of IP addresses that are required to enable the maximum number of concurrent connections that you plan to support on the Client VPN endpoint.
docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/what-is-best-practices
The client CIDR range cannot be changed after you create the Client VPN endpoint.

The subnets associated with a Client VPN endpoint must be in the same VPC.

You cannot associate multiple subnets from the same Availability Zone with a Client VPN endpoint.

not inadvertently sent outside the VPN tunnel

Client Route Enforcement helps enforce administrator-defined routes on devices connected through the VPN. This feature helps improve your security posture by ensuring that network traffic originating from a connected client is not inadvertently sent outside the VPN tunnel.

docs/vpn/latest/clientvpn-admin/disaster-recovery-resiliency
You can associate multiple subnets with a Client VPN endpoint for high availability.

you must manage the software appliance, including configuration, patches, and upgrades
a potential single point of failure into the network design because the software VPN appliance runs on a single Amazon EC2 instance
scope: software VPN appliance on Amazon EC2
ev: docs/whitepapers/latest/aws-vpc-connectivity-options/software-vpn

This option is recommended if you must manage both ends of the VPN connection, either for compliance purposes or for leveraging gateway devices that are not currently supported by Amazon VPC’s VPN solution.

claim: When VPN connections end on a transit gateway, ECMP aggregates multiple VPN tunnels for higher bandwidth, and it requires dynamic routing in the VPN connections; ECMP is not supported with static routing.
q: What routing does ECMP across VPN tunnels need on a transit gateway?
v: To use ECMP, you need to configure dynamic routing in the VPN connections
ECMP is not supported using static routing
scope: Site-to-Site VPN on a transit gateway
ev: docs/whitepapers/latest/aws-vpc-connectivity-options/aws-transit-gateway-vpn

When terminating the VPN connections in the Transit Gateway, you can use Equal Cost Multi-Path (ECMP) routing to get a higher VPN bandwidth by aggregating multiple VPN tunnels. To use ECMP, you need to configure dynamic routing in the VPN connections – ECMP is not supported using static routing.

claim: VPN connection-hours are billed for any time your VPN connections are in the available state. To avoid further charges you terminate the VPN connection.
q: When are Site-to-Site VPN connection-hours billed?
v: VPN connection-hours are billed for any time your VPN connections are in the "available" state
you simply terminate the VPN connection to avoid being billed for additional VPN connection-hours
ev: www/vpn/faqs

VPN connection-hours are billed for any time your VPN connections are in the "available" state. You can determine the state of a VPN connection via the AWS Management Console, CLI, or API. If you no longer wish to use your VPN connection, you simply terminate the VPN connection to avoid being billed for additional VPN connection-hours.

claim: An accelerated Site-to-Site VPN connection pays the normal VPN connection price plus hourly charges for two Global Accelerators per connection and Data Transfer Out Premium fees. Non-accelerated VPNs have no Global Accelerator charges.
q: What extra charges does an accelerated Site-to-Site VPN add?
v: hourly charges for two Global Accelerators per VPN connection and Data Transfer Out Premium (DT-Premium) fees
You will not incur any AWS Global Accelerator charges for non-accelerated VPNs
ev: www/vpn/pricing

If you enable acceleration when creating an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to your Amazon VPC, Site-to-Site VPN connection pricing will apply as indicated above. You will also incur hourly charges for two Global Accelerators per VPN connection and Data Transfer Out Premium (DT-Premium) fees. DT-Premium depends on the source (AWS Region) and the destination (the edge location). See the AWS Global Accelerator pricing page. You will not incur any AWS Global Accelerator charges for non-accelerated VPNs.

claim: Each Site-to-Site VPN connection uses unique public IPv4 addresses for its tunnels, and you incur standard public IPv4 address charges for them.
q: Does a Site-to-Site VPN connection add public IPv4 address charges?
v: Each Site-to-Site VPN connection uses unique public IPv4 address for the tunnels
You will incur standard public IPv4 address charges on the IPv4 address that will be used for the tunnels
ev: www/vpn/pricing
Each Site-to-Site VPN connection uses unique public IPv4 address for the tunnels. You will incur standard public IPv4 address charges on the IPv4 address that will be used for the tunnels.

claim: A VPN Concentrator is charged for each Concentrator-hour that it is provisioned and available. In addition, you are charged for each VPN connection-hour of connections through the Concentrator, plus standard data transfer charges.
q: What do you pay for with a Site-to-Site VPN Concentrator?
v: you are charged for each VPN Concentrator-hour that your VPN Concentrator is provisioned and available
you are also charged for each VPN connection-hour that your VPN connection (via VPN Concentrator) is provisioned and available
ev: www/vpn/pricing

If you create an AWS Site-to-Site VPN Concentrator you are charged for each VPN Concentrator-hour that your VPN Concentrator is provisioned and available. Additionally, you are also charged for each VPN connection-hour that your VPN connection (via VPN Concentrator) is provisioned and available.
